### 2026-10-08 – Hi!!!! I was planning to make a reel, but I'm running out of time 😭 (#gatedbydaven ✌️), so I have to be quick. This was yesterday (Wednesday); before half-life started, I did the warm-up week to get

**3h**

Hi!!!! I was planning to make a reel, but I'm running out of time 😭 (#gatedbydaven ✌️), so I have to be quick. This was yesterday (Wednesday); before half-life started, I did the warm-up week to get into hardware, which is why I’m not working on starbie during this first week of PCB design. So, I decided to build a USB hub that I named SCH (for Super Cool Hub). I’ve already put together a basic BOM, since that’s my main hurdle. Being in Ecuador, electronic components and hardware are quite expensive here, as are import duties. How I'm actually building it on week 5, I've to think right about it.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/gIDkxfUvN4uQnTurIE7oSxqjiiMUakDr/56845ac98f1a408eafbb1ad958e13aa0f606faee21664500da2111abc9532518.png)

Anyways, I'm still a beginner here, so if u think that 3 hours researching, planning and looking 4 components on my own is too much, I'm sorry, but iI barely know anything about components (that's not in any guide)

Listen to my plan: the main chip of this project is the ESP32 S2/S3 DevKitC, why? cus it has the OTG USB interface I need, otherwise I'd to design a more complex PCBA to which I don't have the money or experience neither.

![esp32s3](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/gIDkxfUvN4uQnTurIE7oSxqjiiMUakDr/a26e3aa9a27169165c8c7952b46fcbfe6bb3cc1cfa3462c5418f0c1b9bdf7609.png)

Then, I'm gonna have 3 ports with OLED monochrome screens that hopefully (cause the esp32 is gonna be managing a lot of traffic through usb) will display data and tactile buttons to desactivate power/data transfer for each one. I know I need some diodes in case a port generate an electric charge to prevent ruin the esp32 or even my host usb port (where all energy is gonna be coming and data transfered)

![display](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/gIDkxfUvN4uQnTurIE7oSxqjiiMUakDr/e5e7ffb7abdf330aa825ac4f6fced734c809218bc680a8fb88b6532211c3e501.jpg)

That's all for now, now I'm gonna do the PCB design (please someone teach me to use OpenShape to design CADs :sob:)

### 2026-10-11 – Hi!!! Second work session :) I got locked in today from 4 am until about 1 pm, though after breakfast, lunch, etc, it ended up being around 7 hours of actual work. I already had a plan in mind and a p

**7h**

Hi!!! Second work session :) I got locked in today from 4 am until about 1 pm, though after breakfast, lunch, etc, it ended up being around 7 hours of actual work. I already had a plan in mind and a preliminary BOM, and so on. I started by placing the two main chips: the CH334F and the ESP32 S3 WROOM. I don't think I mentioned this in the previous post, but the reason for choosing these two components is that the ESP32 S3 supports USB OTG (On-The-Go); this meant the CH334F would act as a hub for the ESP32 and the other USB ports. The first connections I made between them were the DM (-) and DP (+) lines to establish the hub configuration. Then I ran into an issue: I was using the WROOM module itself rather than the DevKit (which usually comes with its own voltage regulator), so I had to step down the CH334F's 5V output to 3.3V to power up the microcontroller.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/gIDkxfUvN4uQnTurIE7oSxqjiiMUakDr/59cd56313c7fc2c765e787574fa88a56d06419b90e87f4fda9bdf53a633ff63e.png)

Next came the Enable/Reset pin setup, which involved a resistor and a capacitor discharging to ground. After that, to toggle between running and memory flashing for the ESP32, I wired a switch to GPIO0 to select between 3.3V and GND. Then I added resistors and capacitors around the CH334F pins, for instance, to configure it to always connect to a computer, to add a ready indicator LED, and to set up a couple of ground connections. Once the two main chips were sorted out, the only thing left was to connect the USB-A ports to the CH334F pins, hooking up the 5V, GND, DP, and DM lines.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/gIDkxfUvN4uQnTurIE7oSxqjiiMUakDr/784df99040482824db4a4de9e0603a94e34b781938a42ca3bc2f648c4d645b88.png)

Once I got to that point, I did worry that it might run short on power in certain situations. That’s why I planned from the start to add an auxiliary power line. I ended up implementing this using diodes and the SparkFun DEV-14050, which uses the CH340G chip and, unlike the actual chip, it can output 5V (with a jumper), so I was able to tie them together.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/gIDkxfUvN4uQnTurIE7oSxqjiiMUakDr/8c6e8eb91787e0952fde8d53e229c92f4212a65e45e4e59ae2e31acc52fdfb8b.png)

And that was the process behind my PCB. I know I didn't get around to the OLED screens, but that would have required a coprocessor (which was beyond my scope in terms of complexity, time, and cost), so for a first hardware project without a tutorial, I think it turned out well. It was perhaps a bit challenging, but that was the whole point of the project. I mean, at first I thought, "An USB hub should be easy, just connect the host, the hub, etc, like a bridge; plus, they're cheap, so how complex could it be?" But then I started looking at references and examples and realized that the ones on the market cost over $100, which was sus. Anyway, that was my PCB design project for the first week (I'll try to upload another project right now if I can do it quickly, one involving sensors and an exhaust fan to relax :))
